about: Lesson F10's own inputs: six real energy balances (the United States, the European Union, China, India, Brazil and Norway), each as its national statistics office or the EU's statistics office published it, one data year per country, with the rows used, the units and the conversions; the accounting conventions; the four lenses; the regional card each country opens; the numbers to remember. Every value here was read on the cited page or table between 2 and 7 November 2026. Prairieland's numbers are read from prairieland.json at run time, never copied here.
subEffNote: Set for teaching: the substitution method counts each MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar as the fuel a thermal plant would burn to make it, at an assumed efficiency; publishers have used different efficiencies in different years, so the page uses one round value, 40%, for every real country (Prairieland uses its own fleet's, from its file).

countries.name: United States
countries.otherNote: geothermal (0.12 quads) and the rest of EIA's total
countries.published: 96.5 quads of primary energy consumption; EIA counts nuclear at its plants' heat rate and hydro, wind and solar at the heat content of their electricity (3,412 Btu per kWh) since September 2023, close to the physical energy content method; fossil fuels at their gross heat content.
notes: End-use energy without electrical system losses (Tables 2.2 to 2.5); EIA's 6.5 quads of non-fuel use, mostly in industry, are shown apart as non-energy use.
Agriculture is inside EIA's industrial sector, so no farm row.
countries.resources: Crude oil, natural gas and coal.
countries.institutions: 7 ISO/RTO markets plus vertically integrated utilities; 3 weakly coupled interconnections.

countries.name: European Union (27 countries)
countries.otherNote: ambient heat for heat pumps, geothermal, non-renewable waste and electricity and heat trade
countries.published: 55,790 PJ of gross available energy, by the physical energy content method: nuclear as reactor heat; hydro, wind and solar photovoltaic as their electricity.
notes: Coal includes peat and oil shale; solar includes solar heat (164 PJ); bioenergy is renewables less hydro, wind, solar, geothermal, tide and ambient heat.
Gross available energy includes 1,704 PJ of fuel for international shipping, shown apart.
Electricity by source is gross production (nrg_bal_peh).

importDep.text: Eurostat's import dependency rate: net imports ÷ gross available energy

production.split: renewables 48.1%, nuclear heat 28.2%, oil 3.3% and natural gas 5.1% of that production

countries.institutions: Unbundled zonal markets, coupled day-ahead and intraday; dense interconnection.

countries.name: China
countries.published: 571,327 × 10,000 t of coal equivalent (5.71 billion t, about 167 EJ): coal 54.8%, oil 18.8%, gas 8.5%, primary electricity and other energy 17.9%; electricity from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar is counted at the coal burned per kWh in the year's thermal plants (the coal-equivalent method).
countries.noFinal: China's statistics count the electricity users buy at the coal burned to make it, so its final energy cannot be drawn on the same basis as the others; this page shows its primary energy only.
notes: Physical energy content here is the page's estimate: fossil fuels as published, plus nuclear, hydro, wind and solar from their TWh; the 'other energy' in NBS's 17.9% is not split by NBS and is left out.
Solar generation from the 2023 Statistical Communiqué; the rest from the 2025 Statistical Yearbook (2023 data).

importDep.text: net imports ÷ total energy consumption, both in coal equivalent

countries.institutions: State-owned grids; provincial dispatch; spot markets moving toward a unified market.

countries.name: India
countries.published: 903,158 ktoe (37,813 PJ) of total primary energy supply; hydro, wind and solar at their electricity (1 GWh = 0.086 ktoe), nuclear at its electricity ÷ 0.33.
notes: Coal includes lignite; oil is crude oil less net exports of oil products.
The balance has no row for firewood or other traditional biomass.
Wind, solar and other renewable electricity includes bio-power and small hydro (not split in the tables read).
'Other' final use is agriculture and the balance's non-specified other uses.
countries.institutions: State distribution companies (DISCOMs) buy under long-term contracts; one synchronous grid.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.published: 328.5 Mtep of domestic energy supply (Oferta Interna de Energia); hydro, wind and solar at their electricity (1 kWh = 860 kcal), nuclear at its electricity ÷ 0.33.
notes: Bioenergy is sugarcane products (52.0), firewood and charcoal (27.1), and black liquor and other renewables (29.2), in Mtep.
Hydro includes imported electricity; solar includes solar heat.

BEN's final consumption includes the energy sector's own use; the page moves it to 'before the meter', as the other countries count it. Services, farms and the energy sector are split by their published shares.
countries.institutions: Hydro-dominated national grid; cost-based dispatch; auctions plus a free market.

countries.name: Norway
countries.published: 326 TWh of net domestic energy supply (Table 2; its rows add to 326.2); electricity at its own energy content (1 MWh = 3.6 GJ).
notes: Electricity in the supply is production less net exports; its hydro, wind and solar are not split in the balance (hydro made 89.9% of 2025's generation).
Bioenergy and waste: biofuels 19.5 and waste 5.2 TWh.
Buildings here are households only: services sit in 'other' with farms and fishing.

importDep.text: net imports ÷ net domestic energy supply

countries.resources: Oil and gas, mostly for export; rivers for its own electricity.
countries.institutions: Nord Pool bidding zones; flow-based market coupling since October 2024; hydro and dense HVDC links.

prairieland.name: Prairieland
prairieland.institutions: Fictional: the course does not set out its institutions.

conventions.label: Physical energy content
conventions.who: the IEA and Eurostat, and five of the six statistics offices on this page (China's is the exception)
conventions.text: Nuclear counts as its reactors' heat (electricity ÷ 0.33); hydro, wind and solar as the electricity they make.

conventions.label: Substitution
conventions.who: the Energy Institute's former method; China's coal-equivalent method is one kind
conventions.text: Every MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fuel a thermal plant would burn to make it.

conventions.label: Direct equivalent
conventions.text: Every MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts at its electricity, 3.6 GJ.
conventions.note: A lower bound: no conversion losses counted for any of them.

lenses.label: Import dependence
lenses.text: net imports as a share of primary energy: high for countries with few fuels of their own.

lenses.label: Resources
lenses.text: what the country produces at home: rivers, coal, oil, gas, crops.

lenses.label: Climate
lenses.text: buildings' share of final energy: heating and cooling raise it, and so do bigger homes, higher incomes and how statistics group services; the table cannot tell these apart.

lenses.label: Institutions
lenses.text: who runs the power system and how electricity is traded, from the regional cards.
